34.0.s.en: 1. A call to those present to listen

34.0.0.en: 1 Furthermore Elihu answered and said, 2 "Hear my words, O ye wise men; and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge. 3 For the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat. 4 Let us choose to us judgment: let us know among ourselves what is good.

34.0.2.en: "Answered": this does not mean that someone asked and Elihu answered him. Scripture is accustomed to begin speeches with this word, "answered," even if no one has spoken before, as in (Job 3:2; Isa 14:10; Zech 1:10; 3:4; 4:11-12). Sometimes this word is used to express an answer to a hidden question in the mind of another person, an opponent, who has not disclosed it openly.

34.1.0.en: Hear my words, O ye wise men; and give ear unto me, ye that have knowledge [2].

34.1.1.en: In the previous chapter Elihu addressed his speech to Job, answering his questions about sorrows and tribulations, explaining that they are by God's permission for the benefit of believers, since the believer is given the opportunity to withdraw into himself, discover his faults, and seek the one divine Mediator. Job did not answer him, nor did he comment on his words. Now he addresses his speech particularly to his three friends, calling them wise, men who have been given knowledge. In this he wanted to prepare them to listen to him attentively and without hostility. Perhaps he looked upon them as truly wise, able to follow his words and his explanation of some difficult matters.

34.2.0.en: For the ear trieth words, as the mouth tasteth meat [3].

34.2.1.en: Elihu calls us to have a spirit of discernment. As the mouth tastes food and distinguishes what is good from what is spoiled, so it is fitting for our ears to separate good words from evil ones. Here he speaks to those present, especially the three friends, and he speaks not only of the inner ears but also of the bodily ears, so that believers may not leave the doors of their ears open to receive all words without discrimination.

34.2.2.en: Just as we shall be judged for an idle word that wastes our time, we must be on guard against every word we hear, and flee as far as we can from listening not only to what is evil but also to what is vain and useless.

34.2.3.en: Many of the Fathers see that negligence in listening to the dissolute or to heretics may corrupt the purity of the soul and the uprightness of faith. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to test what is said and not allow his ears to listen without discernment.

34.2.4.en: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" (2 Cor 13:5).

34.2.5.en: "Prove all things; hold fast that which is good" (1 Thess 5:21).

34.2.6.en: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world" (1 Jn 4:1).

34.2.8.en: "To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues" (1 Cor 12:10).

34.2.9.en: "But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil" (Heb 5:14).

34.2.10.en: * "Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines" (Heb 13:9). This is the meaning of discerning between good and evil. [The mouth tastes food, but the soul tests words] (see Job 34:3).

34.2.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * Discernment is better than all the virtues.

34.2.12.en: The Spiritual Elder * [Lord, by thy favour thou hast made my mountain to stand strong] (Ps 30:7)... Some ask about the results of virtue... Some say that every virtue has a cause (reason), while others reject this explanation... For example, the aim or cause of wisdom is to distinguish between good and evil... and by discernment we are able to choose and to refuse, and by justice we perceive what we ought to give and what we ought not to give... by courage we perceive what we ought to fear and what we ought not to fear... As for the virtues of beauty and strength, they have no cause... rather their value comes from other virtues that have a cause... For the wise perceive what beauty is through the harmony and order within their souls... and they perceive strength through the practical carrying out of theoretical virtue.

34.2.13.en: St. Basil the Great * My son, do not speak in anger, but let your speech be with wisdom and knowledge, and likewise your silence, because the speech of our wise fathers was full of wisdom and discernment, and likewise their silence.

34.3.0.en: St. Anthony the Great * Let us choose to us judgment: let us know among ourselves what is good [4].

34.3.1.en: Let us test matters for ourselves, not concerned with the praise of others; what occupies us is to reach the truth, to know the facts, and to strive to find what is good.

34.3.2.en: It is fitting for the believer to strive to discover what is true, what is just, and what belongs to the sons, amid conflicting opinions and concepts, testing everything with seriousness and sincerity, without partiality to his own opinions or the opinions of those who love him.

34.3.3.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that it is fitting for us to examine ourselves, listening to the voice of the Lord Christ who is within us, as well as to His voice in the holy Church through our Church teachers.

34.3.4.en: * Look within yourselves, and you will find Christ in you. But if Christ is in you, how much more is He in your teacher.

34.3.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * If we do not know how one is to examine another, we do not know whether Christ is in us or not. Failure to practice examination is ignorance of the faith inherited in the declaration of our faith. Whoever has the sense of faith in his heart knows that Jesus Christ is in him.

34.3.6.en: Ambrosiaster * As in ancient Israel there were some prophets who spoke the word of God and others who did not, so too, as soon as the apostles appeared speaking in Christ and having the Holy Spirit whom the Lord sent to them, Satan sent many false apostles who falsified the teaching of the Gospel. It is vital that you have the gift of the Holy Spirit that is called the discerning of spirits, so that you may test the spirits and see what you must believe and what you must reject.

34.3.7.en: St. Didymus the Blind * We must observe this threefold matter with all care: let us examine the thoughts that attack us with insight and wisdom, so that we may know the source of the thought and its causes from its beginning. In this way we can consider whether we should yield to it, according to the kind of one who proposes it, and so be like the wise money-changers, as the Lord teaches us. By their skill and experience they distinguish the pure gold that has been purified by fire as it ought to be, and by their skill they are not deceived by pieces of copper coated with a thin layer of gold which appear to be of great value... By their intelligence and skill they perfectly recognize the counterfeit coins minted by the great deceivers...

34.3.8.en: So we must first examine with all care every thought that enters our hearts and every teaching that we receive, to see whether it has been purified by the fire of the divine, heavenly Holy Spirit, or belongs to the error of the heretics, or is the fruit of the pride of human philosophy, which has nothing but the outward appearance of religion.

34.3.9.en: We can do this if we walk by the counsel of the Apostle who says: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God..." (1 Jn 4:1). Some are deceived by this kind of thing, enticed by fine arrangement and by philosophical teachings that deceive at first glance with some pious meanings that agree with religion, just as the gleam of gold deceives the eyes. Appearances attract these people, but they soon feel that in fact they have come away empty-handed, and they fall into despair, like those who have been deceived by counterfeit copper coins.

34.4.s.en: 2. A reply to Job's justifying himself

34.4.0.en: 5 "For Job hath said, I am righteous: and God hath taken away my judgment. 6 Should I lie against my right? my wound is incurable without transgression. 7 What man is like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water? 8 Which goeth in company with the workers of iniquity, and walketh with wicked men. 9 For he hath said, It profiteth a man nothing that he should delight himself with God. 10 "Therefore hearken unto me, ye men of understanding: far be it from God, that he should do wickedness; and from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity. 11 For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways. 12 Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment.

34.4.2.en: I am righteous: and God hath taken away my judgment [5].

34.4.3.en: These words came in Job (Job 13:18; 27:2), but he said them to clear himself, because his friends had attacked him personally, so he wanted to affirm his innocence of the false accusations, without meaning that he was justified before God or that he was free from error. He never hinted that he was always pure of heart or that he never sinned against the law of his Creator. He truly said that God had taken away his judgment, but he never meant that he wished to take God to court, accusing Him of injustice; rather, what he meant was that God was dealing with him in a secret, mysterious way, and not as he had been accustomed to feel in his relationship with Him before, in terms of His surpassing divine providence. What was mysterious to him was not the trials that had befallen him, but how He allowed his friends to stumble over him.

34.4.4.en: Job had confessed his sins, but he bears a relative righteousness when compared with his brothers in humanity, not when compared with God. For it has been said: "For there is not a just man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not" (Eccl 7:20).

34.4.5.en: * I know no man perfect in anything... being still a man, except the One who alone for our sake put on our humanity.

34.4.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * God is good, perfectly good alone, and since you are His image, it is fitting for you to be good. He is generous to all, so you ought to be generous, avoiding greed, and not withholding from your neighbor anything material and transitory, for this is the gravest disaster and folly.

34.4.7.en: Father John of Kronstadt * First return to yourself from what is outside you; then present yourself again to Him who created you. For He is the source of all our happiness and perfect goodness.

34.4.8.en: St. Augustine * Should I lie against my right?

34.5.0.en: My wound is incurable without transgression [6].

34.5.1.en: Perhaps Job is asking: Should he lie and accuse himself of evil as his friends think, and so become a liar against his declaration of innocence of what they ascribed to him?

34.5.2.en: He cries out, for his wound has become incurable though he committed no iniquity. They accused him of being the worst criminal and treated him in the most terrible way, although God Himself testified to his perfection, and that Satan had incited Him against him without cause (Job 1:1; 2:3).

34.5.3.en: By his wound here he means the calamities that befell him, which seemed incurable, with no remedy for them and no possibility of mending the situation.

34.5.4.en: The picture here is that Job is like an animal struck by a deadly arrow through no fault of its own. What Job complains of is not that he is without sin, but of the calamities that have befallen him, which completely distorted his image, especially in the minds of his friends.

34.6.0.en: What man is like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water? [7]

34.6.1.en: Some see that this proverb suits the ancient desert environment, as it likens the man to a camel that drinks a huge quantity of water that enables it not to feel thirst for a long time during its journey in the dry wilderness. So Job drank huge quantities of trials, whose effect continues throughout his whole journey here in the wilderness of this world.

34.6.2.en: Eliphaz cited a similar phrase when accusing Job (Job 15:16).

34.7.0.en: Which goeth in company with the workers of iniquity, and walketh with wicked men? [8]

34.7.1.en: Elihu reckoned Job a companion of the wicked, because he bore thoughts like theirs in his complaint with God (Job 9:22-23, 30; 21:7-15), at least in saying that those who do evil are not punished. It seems as though he denied God's justice because of his not knowing what lay behind the tribulations that befell him while they did not befall the wicked, so Elihu counted him as one who by his thoughts befriended the wicked.

34.8.0.en: For he hath said, It profiteth a man nothing that he should delight himself with God [9].

34.8.1.en: Since Job adopted this thought in the bitterness of his soul, saying that there is no profit in serving God, and that a man's walking in righteousness profits him nothing, because God does not defend the righteous against those who oppose them, Elihu therefore reckoned Job to be in friendship with the wicked.

34.8.2.en: Therefore hearken unto me, ye men of understanding.

34.9.0.en: Far be it from God, that he should do wickedness; and from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity [10].

34.9.1.en: Elihu calls those present to listen to his answer to what he thought were mistaken concepts on Job's part, showing that Job used improper expressions in his complaint with God concerning His judgments.

34.9.2.en: "Ye men of understanding": the Hebrew word means "hearts," for the Jews considered the heart to be the center of all mental processes and their throne. They did not speak of the mind or the head as the throne of mental processes. So Elihu reckons those present to be wise, and able to grasp the thought he presents concerning God's righteousness and justice in His judgments.

34.9.3.en: Elihu wants to affirm that far be it from God to err or to do evil.

34.9.4.en: Elihu says: We must not place God's actions on human scales, so that we sometimes accuse Him of injustice. Rather, it is fitting for us to trust that all God's ways are true and just, because they are His ways and He is holy, and not because we see them so.

34.9.5.en: "What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? God forbid" (Rom 9:14).

34.9.6.en: "That be far from thee to do after this manner, to slay the righteous with the wicked: and that the righteous should be as the wicked, that be far from thee: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" (Gen 18:25).

34.9.7.en: "He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he" (Deut 32:4).

34.9.8.en: "Righteous art thou, O Lord, and all thy judgments are right, and all thy ways mercy and truth and judgment" (Tob 3:2).

34.9.9.en: "God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day" (Ps 7:11).

34.9.10.en: "For the righteous Lord loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright" (Ps 11:7).

34.9.11.en: "The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring for ever: the judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether" (Ps 19:9).

34.9.12.en: "The righteousness of thy testimonies is everlasting: give me understanding, and I shall live" (Ps 119:144).

34.9.13.en: "Seeing then that thou art righteous thyself, thou orderest all things righteously: thinking it not agreeable with thy power to condemn him that hath not deserved to be punished" (Wis 12:15).

34.9.14.en: "Therefore the Lord hath watched over us for evil, and the Lord hath brought it upon us: for the Lord is righteous in all his works which he hath commanded us" (Bar 2:9).

34.9.15.en: "For thou art just in all that thou hast done, and all thy works are true, and thy ways right, and all thy judgments truth" (Additions to Dan 3:27).

34.9.16.en: "The just Lord is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame" (Zeph 3:5).

34.9.17.en: "And this is what Nehemiah prayed: O Lord, Lord God, Creator of all things, who art fearful and strong, and righteous, and merciful, and the only and gracious King" (2 Macc 1:24).

34.9.18.en: "The only giver of all things, the only just, almighty, and eternal, thou that deliverest Israel from all trouble, and didst choose the fathers, and sanctify them" (2 Macc 1:25).

34.9.19.en: "And I heard the angel of the waters say, Thou art righteous, O Lord, which art, and wast, and shalt be, because thou hast judged thus" (Rev 16:5).

34.9.20.en: "And I heard another out of the altar say, Even so, Lord God Almighty, true and righteous are thy judgments" (Rev 16:7).

34.9.21.en: "For true and righteous are his judgments: for he hath judged the great whore, which did corrupt the earth with her fornication, and hath avenged the blood of his servants at her hand" (Rev 19:2).

34.9.22.en: * If He whom you call Father is our Judge, and if He is no respecter of persons, then let us hasten and give all diligence during our journey here on earth, in all fear and holy conduct... By this we know that this same Father is the One who gives us the promises, and He is the One who keeps us without any punishment.

34.9.23.en: St. Didymus the Blind * God is a righteous, strong, and longsuffering Judge. Do you not understand why He does not punish although He is able and ready? He says: Learn that He is longsuffering, and does not give vent to His anger every day. Behold, you see that, lest some fool think that God holds back out of weakness, He shows that the reason for His delay is His very wide longsuffering. I mean that He is longsuffering in order to lead you to repentance, and if you do not benefit from this remedy, He will take action also. Be sure that we deserve punishment every day... Does a day pass without our praying with indifference and a dangerous distraction of mind?

34.9.24.en: St. John Chrysostom * Those who forsake God, despise His commandments, and bring shame on their Creator by their deeds and by their thoughts that blaspheme the One who sustains them, gather just judgment against themselves.

34.10.0.en: St. Irenaeus * For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways [11].

34.10.1.en: God always acts with justice; He will not forget the righteous, nor allow the wicked to prosper in the end. He will deal with every man according to his deserving.

34.10.2.en: He did not mean by this that he judges Job to be wicked because of what has befallen him, as his three friends accused him, but he thinks he is correcting an obscure or mistaken concept of Job that he expressed in the bitterness of his soul.

34.10.3.en: Let us wait, for God will reward the righteous and also repay the wicked if they persist in their evils, at the proper time. The Lord said of the wicked king Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah: [They shall not lament for him, saying, Ah my brother! or, Ah sister! they shall not lament for him, saying, Ah lord! or, Ah his glory! He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem] (Jer 22:18-19). It was also said: "But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God; who will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:5-6). "And if ye call on the Father, who without respect of persons judgeth according to every man's work, pass the time of your sojourning here in fear" (1 Pet 1:17). "And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according to his work shall be" (Rev 22:12).

34.10.4.en: * Why does God not punish all men with mercy in such a way that He allows no one to harden himself against Him? (This question arises) because of the evil to which those who have become hardened have qualified themselves, or because of God's mysterious judgments, which are often hidden but will never be unjust.

34.11.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles * Yea, surely God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment [12].

34.11.1.en: Elihu repeats this principle, affirming that God does no evil, and speaking of it at length. Under all circumstances this principle cannot be breached, not even for a single moment. He found fault with Job because, although he embraced the same principle, under the pressure of intense sufferings he thought that God could err in His judgment, so that injustice would take the place of justice (Job 34:5; 8:3).

34.11.2.en: The Lord said to Satan: "Thou movedst me against him, to destroy him without cause" (Job 2:3). And as Pope Gregory (the Great) says, God may allow sorrows without a cause (that man deserves), but He will not condemn him without a cause.

34.11.3.en: God allows His righteous ones sorrows for their purification or their approval, but He does not allow them sorrows on the Day of Judgment.

34.11.4.en: * You will obtain the world of light in place of a bitter pain that you bear for Him for one day.

34.11.5.en: If you endure hunger a little for His love's sake, then your desire to see His face will be kindled.

34.11.6.en: If darkness appears on your face from the works done for Him, He will adorn you with His glory forever without end.

34.11.7.en: If you strip yourself of what is yours, He will clothe you with His light, and hide from you what is yours.

34.11.8.en: If you leave what you possess, you will possess it in yourself eternally.

34.11.10.en: * The evils that come upon you will pass, and what you wait for with patience will come.

34.11.11.en: He will wipe away the sweat of toil. He will dry every tear, and there will be no more weeping.

34.11.12.en: Here below we must groan amid trials, as Job asks: [Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth?] (Job 7:1).

34.12.0.en: 13 Who hath given him a charge over the earth? or who hath disposed the whole world? 14 If he set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; 15 All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust. 16 If now thou hast understanding, hear this: hearken to the voice of my words. 17 Shall even he that hateth right govern? and wilt thou condemn him that is most just? 18 Is it fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked? and to princes, Ye are ungodly? 19 How much less to him that accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the rich more than the poor? for they all are the work of his hands. 20 In a moment shall they die, and the people shall be troubled at midnight, and pass away: and the mighty shall be taken away without hand. 21 For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings. 22 There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves. 23 For he will not lay upon man more than right; that he should enter into judgment with God. 24 He shall break in pieces mighty men without number, and set others in their stead. 25 Therefore he knoweth their works, and he overturneth them in the night, so that they are destroyed. 26 He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others; 27 Because they turned back from him, and would not consider any of his ways: 28 So that they cause the cry of the poor to come unto him, and he heareth the cry of the afflicted. 29 When he giveth quietness, who then can make trouble? and when he hideth his face, who then can behold him? whether it be done against a nation, or against a man only: 30 That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.

34.12.1.en: Who hath given him a charge over the earth? or who hath disposed the whole world? [13]

34.12.2.en: He is the Creator of heaven and earth and the Ruler of the whole world; He did not receive His authority from another, nor is He subject to anyone; heaven and earth are the place of His care and delight.

34.12.3.en: If the earth were not the work of His hands, but had been entrusted to Him by another greater than He, He could do wrong and rule unjustly, as one who suffers no harm; but since it is His own, and He is its Creator and the One who cares for it, He governs everything that takes place on earth by His divine justice and His providence that surpasses human understanding. "Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him? Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?" (Job 36:22-23).

34.12.4.en: * Note how Elihu proves the justice of God: [He made the earth] and heaven and all the other creatures. Are His works foreign to Him, that He should be unjust to us...? He is just, not only because these are His works, but because He is their Lord. In fact this happens even with the wicked, for they do not accept harm (from another) coming upon those subject to them. Ordinarily everyone cares for those who are his and what is his. As for Him who is the Creator and Lord, how should He not exercise justice in all His governing, if He has poured out upon it such splendor? You cannot say that He does no injustice out of weakness, for He could easily destroy all men.

34.12.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * He truly governs the world Himself, He who created it Himself. He needs no help from another in governing it, He who needed no help in creating it... If Almighty God did not disdain to govern the world He Himself created, how much more does He govern well what He has created well. He is not harsh toward what He brought into being in His mercy. And He who cared for them before He created them does not abandon them after He has created them.

34.13.0.en: If he set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath [14].

34.13.1.en: Some see that this phrase and the one following mean that if God sets His heart upon a man, He gathers his spirit to Himself, because he is a being very dear to Him. He allows the body to return to dust, but He cherishes the breath He gave him and gathers it to Himself. What intercedes for us all is the love of God who created us and gave us a breath from His mouth. As the wise man says: "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Eccl 12:7).

34.13.2.en: God, in His love for man, sets His heart upon him and focuses His divine plan on his salvation. Truly it is within God's authority to destroy the whole human race, because "They are all gone out of the way, they are together become unprofitable; there is none that doeth good, no, not one" (Rom 3:12). Man no longer has the right to live, and has no standing to ask anything good from God because he disobeyed Him. So whatever befalls man, even death, he cannot complain and accuse God of injustice, for who is justified before Him? As the psalmist says: "Enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified" (Ps 143:2). Yet in His love God allowed the body to die and return to dust, and gathers in His love the spirit of man, granting it the first resurrection with Him, so that in the second resurrection the body also rises with the spirit, and man returns to the divine embrace.

34.13.3.en: In this Elihu answers Job and says to him: Why do you seek a trial before God, for if God examined the life of any man, He would find him a criminal who deserves to be cut off from life completely. It is as though Elihu says to Job: I know that if you are compared with men you are reckoned righteous and perfect, but how do you dare ask to be tried before God, since like all men you deserve death.

34.13.4.en: * [If he set his heart upon him, he will gather unto himself his spirit and his breath] [14]. When the heart seeks lower things it becomes crooked. It becomes upright when it is lifted up to the heavenly things. For if a man sets his heart toward the Lord, the Lord draws his spirit and his breath to Himself. Here he uses the expression "spirit" for the inner thoughts, and the breath that comes out of the body for outward deeds. Thus God draws the spirit and the breath to Himself, in order to change what is within and what is without, making us turn toward Him in our longings... The whole man has burning inner desires toward Him who brought him into being.

34.14.0.en: All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust [15].

34.14.1.en: If God willed, it is His right to remove all humanity; so why do people complain of the loss of health, of temporal goods, or of relatives, and think that God is unjust?

34.14.2.en: * [All flesh shall fall together, and man shall return to dust] [15]. For all flesh falls completely when it is no longer a slave to its passions... So the more a man begins to live for the heavenly things, the more he dies to the lower things... Paul's flesh perished completely when he said: "I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20).

34.14.3.en: Rightly Elihu added in this matter: "man shall turn again unto dust." For everyone who is occupied with sin forgets his mortal condition, and while he is puffed up with pride he does not remember that he is dust. But after the grace of conversion touches him with a spirit of humility, then he recalls to his mind that he is dust.

34.14.4.en: David returned to dust when he said: [Remember, O Lord, that we are dust] (Ps 103:14). And Abraham returned to dust, saying: [I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes] (Gen 18:27). Although death had not yet dissolved the living body into dust, in their own view they were so, as they had foreseen and looked upon it without doubting what would happen.

34.15.0.en: If now thou hast understanding, hear this: hearken to the voice of my words [16].

34.15.1.en: At the beginning of the chapter Elihu addressed his speech to men of wisdom and understanding; now he addresses it rather to Job, if he has understanding. He wanted to rebuke him for the expressions that came from him that were unfitting regarding God and His judgments.

34.16.0.en: Shall even he that hateth right govern? and wilt thou condemn him that is most just? [17]

34.16.1.en: Elihu marvels at man's attitude toward God, that one who is subject to law dares to condemn God, who is all justice and righteousness and the Giver of the law to men.

34.16.2.en: How strange! One who needs a law to govern him puts himself in the position of judge to condemn the Lawgiver. Or one who hates the law and tries to be rid of it wishes to pass judgment on the founder of the law.

34.16.3.en: * He hates evil and loves mankind. He is not like us who leave evil not out of hatred for vice, but out of fear of the coming punishment.

34.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom * Is it fit to say to a king, Thou art wicked? and to princes (to nobles), Ye are ungodly? [18]

34.17.1.en: If God established authorities, it was that they might be honored in the Lord and for the sake of the Lord, and not that they might occupy the Lord's place (Sir 32:1). For a ruler or one in authority whose heart is lifted up in pride falls into apostasy, as happened with Satan. The Apostle Paul, as a leader who feared lest he fall into pride, says: "Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ. But we were gentle among you, even as a nurse cherisheth her children" (1 Thess 2:6-7). The glory of the leader is to bear the Spirit of the Lord, who embraces all who are subject to him with love and treats them as his sons.

34.17.2.en: If man does not dare to accuse an earthly king of wickedness and evil, how can he ascribe injustice and evil to the King of kings and Lord of lords?

34.17.3.en: It is fitting for man to give honor to whom honor is due, for it is hard for a man to judge his rulers, because he does not perceive the hidden causes and secret reasons behind their actions; how then can he condemn the plan of God that is without limit and His plans that surpass the mind.

34.17.4.en: * Now concerning the passages in the Gospel that seem to carry something of contradiction, it is better for each one to rebuke himself that he has not yet attained to understanding "the riches both of the wisdom" (Rom 11:33), and to remember in truth that it is hard to grasp God's mysterious judgments, rather than to accuse them with insolence and rashness, and so hear the words: "It is a lawless one who says: You transgress the law" (Job 34:18) LXX.

34.17.5.en: St. Basil the Great * That accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the rich more than the poor (nor regards the wealthy above the needy).

34.18.0.en: For they all are the work of his hands [19].

34.18.1.en: If it is not fitting for us to judge kings and rulers, who as men often show partiality, how can we condemn God, who treats the rich and the poor on the same level, without respect of persons (see Gal 2:6; Acts 10:34; 2 Chr 19:7; Prov 22:2; Rom 2:11; Eph 6:9; Col 3:25). For all are His creation, and all need His divine providence and mercies in order to enjoy salvation. A man's abilities or position have no bearing on God's dealings with him.

34.18.2.en: * By the ruler or tyrant here is understood every arrogant person, while the humble are indicated by the needy (poor). Therefore God does not favor the tyrant when he opposes the needy, for He declares that He does not know, in the judgment, the proud who trouble the lives of the poor, as it is written: "I know you not whence ye are" (Lk 13:25). If He wished, He could destroy him by His power, since He created him by His power when He willed. Therefore it was fitting to add: "for they all are the work of his hands."

34.19.0.en: In a moment shall they die, and the people shall be troubled at midnight, and pass away: and the mighty (those with power) shall be taken away without hand [20].

34.19.1.en: Here he speaks of three classes in order for Elihu to bring out that God shows no partiality.

34.19.2.en: The first class: the kings and the rich who depend on authority and money, and so are reckoned more secure than others. God not only does not favor these, but sometimes allows their souls to be taken suddenly, something to which the people are not exposed in the same way.

34.19.3.en: The second class: the wicked people, who depend on their great numbers and the strength of walls, when suddenly they suffer troubles and are drawn away from their land, taken captive at midnight. At midnight God struck the firstborn of the Egyptians while they were at ease, mocking the people of God.

34.19.4.en: The third class: the mighty, such as men of war who take pride in their military capabilities; they are sometimes taken away or fall captive from where they do not know, as though without a hand. They are defeated not by a human arm, just as the strong and righteous are not saved by it. As it was said: "This is the word of the Lord unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the Lord of hosts" (Zech 4:6). It was also said: "There is no king saved by the multitude of an host: a mighty man is not delivered by much strength. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength" (Ps 33:16-17).

34.19.5.en: * Let God be your hope, your power of endurance, your strength. Let Him be your atonement, your praise, your goal and place of rest, and your help in your striving...

34.19.6.en: The mighty man is the arrogant man who exalts himself (haughtily) against God, as though he were something in himself and in what is his. Such a man is not saved by his own strength. Now, he has a swift and strong horse, sound and quick of step; if an attack occurs, can it deliver its rider from the danger that besets him? Let him hear: [The horse is a vain thing for safety](a)... You must not let the horse promise you deliverance...

34.19.7.en: We can take the horse as a symbol of any possessions in this world, or any kind of honor on which we rely in pride, wrongly reckoning that the higher you rise, the more your security and your height increase. Do you not realize with what violence you will be thrown down? The higher you climb, the heavier your fall will be... How then is safety achieved? It is not achieved by strength, nor by authority, nor by honor, nor by glory, nor by a horse.

34.20.0.en: St. Augustine * For his eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings [21].

34.20.1.en: God does not need someone to give Him a report about a person, as Job thought when he said: "Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me?" (Job 7:12). Rather the prophet Jeremiah says of Him: "Whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of men" (Jer 32:19), and it was also said of Him: "For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth" (2 Chr 16:9).

34.20.2.en: All things are open before Him, for He is present everywhere, caring for all, exercising divine righteousness and justice. No one escapes from Him (Ps 139:2-3).

34.20.3.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that Elihu affirms God's justice without aiming to harm Job with false accusations as the other three friends did, for he did not say of him that he broke the widows and orphans (Job 22:9). Elihu knows how to blame Job without making accusations against him.

34.20.4.en: "The Lord looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth. He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works" (Ps 33:13-15).

34.20.5.en: "Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? saith the Lord. Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the Lord" (Jer 23:24).

34.20.6.en: * God is reckoned as one who does not know the deeds of the wicked, because He justly postpones their judgment, so that the greatness of His longsuffering toward them appears as a kind of overlooking of them. And the wicked man, each time he sins without being punished, thinks that God does not see him, as a result of not being punished immediately as he deserves. He reckons that his conduct is not hateful to God... But there the punishments will fall upon him suddenly, with an eternal blow. Then he will know that God watches everything, when he finds himself punished by an unexpected death as an eschatological punishment for all his iniquity...

34.20.7.en: * He calls [all the goings of men] either the separate works with which we are occupied, or the successive motives of our deep thoughts, since they are like steps by which we are separated from the Lord or draw near to Him in holiness. For the mind draws near to God as by many steps (degrees) when it advances in many holy affections. Again it is separated from Him through many evil thoughts.

34.21.0.en: There is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves [22].

34.21.1.en: Usually the criminal wants to hide from sight. Elihu says that there is no dark cave here in which the wicked can hide from the eyes of God, and in the world to come there is no deep darkness to which they can flee from His face. A man can hide from the face of his fellow man so that his affair is not exposed, but with God everything is open, whether in this world or on the great day of the Lord. There is a hidden eye that sees the wicked, and a strong hand that draws them to their recompense.

34.21.2.en: "Shadow of death" points to dense darkness (Amos 9:2-3; Ps 139:12).

34.21.3.en: * What does he mean by darkness but ignorance, and by the shadow of death but forgetfulness? Of the ignorance of certain people it is said: "Having the understanding darkened" (Eph 4:18). Again, of the forgetfulness that comes upon us at death it was said: [In that very day his thoughts perish] (Ps 146:4). For all that he thinks of during his life is given over to forgetfulness by death; forgetfulness is a kind of shadow of death, for as the coming of death puts an end to the works of life, so the coming of forgetfulness destroys what is in the memory...

34.21.4.en: No one hides from (God's) judgment; therefore it is impossible for Him not to see what we do, or to forget what He sees... It is the mark of the divine nature alone not to suffer shadows of ignorance or change... For since the eternal light in its shining, which is God Himself, does not change, He sees with a piercing gaze, and is not ignorant of what is hidden, for He penetrates all things, and does not forget what He penetrates since He is unchangeable...

34.21.5.en: When we think that we are not seen, we keep our eyes closed to the light of the sun, meaning we shut it out from us, and do not shut ourselves out from it.

34.22.0.en: For he will not lay upon man more than right; that he should enter into judgment with God [23].

34.22.1.en: Some see that the meaning here is: God does not call man again to trial; He does not look into a case twice, for His judgments are just and need no appeal; the sentence is issued and there is no one to appeal for a fresh pleading.

34.22.2.en: And some translate it: "Behold, no man is given a set time to come to judgment with God." Man's time is not in his hand, nor is his lot fulfilled by his wisdom and strength. When God sees that the time is right, He judges man.

34.23.0.en: He shall break in pieces mighty men without number, and set others in their stead [24].

34.23.1.en: He crushes and shatters those who think themselves great, for He cares nothing for their huge wealth, their standing in society, and their great numbers.

34.23.2.en: "Without number," that is, God does not need long procedures to examine matters and make sure of them. He judges at once, directly, and removes the wicked and sets up those who take their places.

34.23.3.en: In many cases God presses down the proud who are self-reliant, and lifts up the humble and the meek.

34.23.4.en: * [He shall break in pieces many without number, and set others in their stead] [24]. This happens every day, but because the end of the two groups (the righteous and the wicked) has not yet been seen, the awe is less. For the wicked will not know their faults until they fall under punishment... By examining the hearts of men individually, or placing them under justice and mercy, He drives some outside and leads others inside. These others are inspired to seek the inner delights, and He leaves the former to inherit the outer pleasures.

34.23.5.en: He lifts the minds of some toward the heavenly things and casts down the pride of others into the depths of pleasures...

34.23.6.en: He drives out one with firmness, and draws another with His mercy...
